title: Weekly Top Five Articles: You Are Not as Free as You Think You Are
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: This week's Bradley Weekly Top Five gathers five pieces around a single uncomfortable observation: the beliefs we are most certain we chose freely are often the ones handed to us by anxiety, belonging, and the formats that carry them. The five articles cover (1) a Plough essay arguing that the deepest stupidity is moral and volitional -- a refusal to be summoned by the truth -- not intellectual; (2) a Skeptical Inquirer piece on why facts almost never win an argument (people resist correction because a threatened belief feels like a threatened self); (3) a PsyPost study showing that college students abandon their stated free-speech principles the moment a political loyalty is activated; (4) a PsyPost study linking pornography consumption habits to rigid gender beliefs, showing that what we consume for escape doesn't stay inert -- it instructs; and (5) a PsyPost analysis finding that listening to Joe Rogan predicted a 2024 Trump vote more strongly than watching Fox News, because the long-form podcast format builds a one-sided friendship that bypasses the skepticism a newscast would trigger. Bradley's synthesis: we are intuitive creatures who feel first and reason afterward, and our moral instincts are tuned to the group we fear losing -- the cure is not more information but communities that make honesty safe.
points: * The Plough essay's core move is to relocate the problem of stupidity from IQ to will: the most dangerous stupidity is moral -- a comfortable self that works hardest to avoid the humility required to be genuinely unsettled by truth, especially in the educated who already feel morally settled. * Fifty years of science communication confirms that facts almost never change minds on their own because a threatened belief feels like a threatened self -- the implication for leaders and educators is that persuasion requires creating enough psychological safety for someone to afford to be wrong in your presence. * The college students free-speech study is particularly sharp: students hold free-speech principles sincerely until a political loyalty is activated, at which point the principle yields -- the inconsistency is not weakness of character but intensity of belonging, meaning that stated values and operative values are different things that only converge under zero social pressure. * The pornography and gender-beliefs study extends the same insight: what we consume for escape doesn't stay inert but instructs; those who consumed explicit content to avoid difficult feelings drifted most toward rigid, demanding ideals of masculinity and femininity, with the pattern suggesting that rehearsed fantasy slowly becomes conviction. * Bradley's synthesis is the most important take-away: we become what forms us, so the only real freedom is to choose deliberately who gets to do the forming -- communities that can hold disagreement without treating it as betrayal, where people who differ still seek truth together.
quotes: We like to imagine that our convictions are our own, assembled freely from evidence and arrived at by clear thinking. The five pieces gathered here puncture that flattering picture, and they do it from five different directions.

Stupidity, in this account, is not low intelligence but a willful complacency, a refusal to know the truth about oneself and the world. The argument matters because it relocates the problem from the schools to the soul, indicting the educated above all. The person most at risk is the one who already feels well-read and morally settled, because comfort is precisely what dulls the capacity to be summoned by anything true.

People resist correction not because they are foolish but because a threatened belief feels like a threatened self, and the self fights to survive. The author's remedy is telling: stop lecturing and start asking, since questions that surface a person's own contradictions do what assertion cannot.

Only those without a strong side stayed consistent, which suggests that intensity of belonging, not weakness of character, is what bends principle. Beneath the inconsistency lies a familiar anxiety: the fear of betraying one's own people. A principle that protects everyone equally offers no such reassurance, so when the group is watching, the comforting rule wins over the universal one.

The shift these pieces reveal is not that people have become irrational. It is that the conditions under which we form ourselves have quietly changed, and most of us have not noticed who is doing the forming. We become what forms us, so the only real freedom is to choose, deliberately and in good company, who gets to do the forming.
